hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-62927 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-62927, CVE-2026-63252, CVE-2026-58080; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-62927.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-62927 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-62927/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-62927 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-62927')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-62927, CVE-2026-63252, CVE-2026-58080; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('opcuaserverconfig.copy','www.cisa.gov') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-62927, CVE-2026-63252, CVE-2026-58080; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Thermo Fisher Torrent Suite Software
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to read arbitrary files on the Torrent Server. article.summary: On October 5th, Atlassian published patches&#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;for multiple products to fix an "Arbitrary File Access" vulnerability &#;x26;#;x5b; CVE-2026-21589 &#;x26;#;x5d;. An attacker can read arbitrary files in the web application&#;x26;#;39;s directory, potentially exposing sensitive information such as configuration files.
article.raw_text: Scans for Atlassian vulnerablity (CVE-2026-21589), (Wed, Oct 7th) On October 5th, Atlassian published patches&#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;for multiple products to fix an "Arbitrary File Access" vulnerability &#;x26;#;x5b; CVE-2026-21589 &#;x26;#;x5d;. An attacker can read arbitrary files in the web application&#;x26;#;39;s directory, potentially exposing sensitive information such as configuration files. On October 5th, Atlassian published patches for multiple products to fix an "Arbitrary File Access" vulnerability [ CVE-2026-21589 ]. An attacker can read arbitrary files in the web application's directory, potentially exposing sensitive information such as configuration files. This directory traversal vulnerability is a little bit different from the textbook case. Atlassian products replace slashes with the pattern "::". To avoid this issue, but may, in some cases, undo this escape to access files. Watchtowr has a great write-up with all the details and proof-of-concept URLs demonstrating the vulnerability [ Watchtowr ]. Starting yesterday, we saw some exploit attempts hitting our honeypot, using the exploit URLs mentioned in the Watchtowr blog. /download/resources/jira.webresources:color-picker-popup/images/..::..::..::..::..::WEB-INF::web.xml /s/1.0/_/download/resources/com.atlassian.bitbucket.server.bitbucket-webpack-INTERNAL:avatar/avatar/..::..::..::..::..::WEB-INF::urlrewrite.xml /s/1/_/download/resources/com.atlassian.confluence.plugins.dashboard-actions/images/..::..::..::..::..::..::..::..::WEB-INF::web.xml One condition for successful exploitation is that the file the user attempts to access exists. The exploit uses "WEB-INF/web.xml" as it is a required file for Tomcat applications, and can be used similarly to "/etc/passwd". The "/etc/passwd" file will not work in this case. Access is restricted to the web application's directory. The "::" pattern used in the exploit will be translated to "/" on the server, leading to the directory traversal. Based on the timing and the targets hit, I believe these scans are all triggered by the same threat actor. Oddly enough, all the source IPs are associated with Digital Ocean. The source IPs I see from our honeypots: 134.199.229.190 134.199.230.82 137.184.112.247 137.184.33.84 143.198.103.58 143.198.132.93 146.190.169.1 146.190.172.250 159.223.199.218 164.92.68.152 209.38.147.216 24.199.101.184 64.23.172.129 -- Johannes B. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-21589 affecting Atlassian Confluence
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-21589 in Atlassian Confluence within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-21589; vectors: exploit; products: Atlassian Confluence.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Atlassian Confluence
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Atlassian Confluence, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-21589.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Atlassian Confluence' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-21589 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-21589/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-21589 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-21589')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Atlassian Confluence hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-21589; vectors: exploit; products: Atlassian Confluence.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('jira.webresources','web.xml','com.atlassian.bitbucket.server.bitbucket') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('134.199.229.190','134.199.230.82','137.184.112.247') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-21589; vectors: exploit; products: Atlassian Confluence.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Hitachi Energy RTU500
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is publishing this cybersecurity advisory in response to the security findings reported by Dragos affecting end-of-life RTU500 CMU firmware version 9.x. The reported findings are associated with legacy RTU500 firmware versions that were developed according to the cybersecurity requirements, threat landscape, and industry practices that existed at the time of their release. As cybersecurity threats and security expectations have evolved, these end-of-life versions no longer incorporate many of the security controls and hardening measures that are standard in modern industrial control systems. Over successive RTU500 releases, Hitachi Energy has continuously enhanced the security of the product through the introduction of additional security features, protocol hardening, stronger authentication and access controls, encrypted communications, and other security-by-design improvements. While the findings reported by Dragos do not affect currently supported RTU500 CMU firmware versions, there is a likelihood that the end-of-life versions 11.x and prior are affected by these vulnerabilities. Since the end-of-life versions are no longer maintained with security updates, Hitachi Energy strongly recommends upgrading to a currently supported RTU500 firmware version. Customers should also implement appropriate defense-in-depth measures and cybersecurity best practices to reduce risk and strengthen the security posture of their operational environments. Ple

General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. article.raw_text: Microsoft, Adobe, Apple, and Foxit vulnerabilities Cisco Talos’ Vulnerability Discovery & Research team recently disclosed vulnerabilities in Adobe, Apple, Foxit Reader, and Microsoft. The vulnerabilities mentioned in this blog post have been patched by their respective vendors, in adherence to Cisco’s third-party vulnerability disclosure policy . For Snort coverage that can detect Cisco Talos’ Vulnerability Discovery & Research team recently disclosed vulnerabilities in Adobe, Apple, Foxit Reader, and Microsoft. The vulnerabilities mentioned in this blog post have been patched by their respective vendors, in adherence to Cisco’s third-party vulnerability disclosure policy . For Snort coverage that can detect the exploitation of these vulnerabilities, download the latest rule sets from Snort.org , and our latest Vulnerability Advisories are always posted on Talos Intelligence’s website . Adobe Photoshop privilege escalation vulnerability TALOS-2026-2360 (CVE-2026-48388) is a privilege escalation vulnerability in the Installation functionality of Photoshop (version(s): Photoshop_Set-Up.exe version 2.11.0.30). An attacker can replace files with a specially crafted malformed file to trigger this vulnerability and lead to privilege escalation. Apple macOS CoreWLAN information disclosure vulnerability TALOS-2026-2376 is an information disclosure vulnerability in the CoreWLAN functionality of macOS (version(s): 26.3.1(25D2128)). An attacker can call a sequence of APIs to trigger this vulnerability. Foxit Reader code execution and use-after-free vulnerabilities TALOS-2026-2420 (CVE-2026-57256) is a code execution vulnerability in the Javascript checkbox CBF_Widget functionality of Foxit Reader (version(s): 2026.1.1.36485). A specially crafted malformed file provided by an attacker can lead to remote code execution. TALOS-2026-2446 (CVE-2026-91799) is a use-after-free vulnerability in the way Foxit Reader handles an Array object. A specially crafted JavaScript code inside a malicious PDF document can trigger this vulnerability, which can lead to memory corruption and result in arbitrary code execution. Microsoft Windows out-of-bounds, use-after-free, and type confusion vulnerabilities TALOS-2026-2443 (CVE-2026-50475) is an out-of-bounds pointer offset vulnerability in the Microsoft Windows NETIO.sys driver. A specially crafted I/O request packet (IRP) can cause disclosure of sensitive information. TALOS-2026-2426 (CVE-2026-58613) is a use-after-free vulnerability in Windows Cloud Files Mini Filter Driver (version(s): 10.0.26100.8457 (WinBuild.160101.0800)). A specially crafted sequence of Cloud Filter API calls, executed with a dedicated application, can lead to privilege escalation. TALOS-2026-2445 (CVE-2026-80093) is a type confusion vulnerability in Windows Cloud Files Mini Filter Driver (version(s): 10.0.26100.8457 (WinBuild.160101.0800) and 10.0.26100.8655 (WinBuild.160101.0800)). A specially crafted sequence of Cloud Filter API calls can lead to type confusion. An attacker can execute a dedicated application to trigger this vulnerability. TALOS-2026-2427 (CVE-2026-49177) is an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in Microsoft Windows tcpip.sys driver. A specially crafted I/O request packet (IRP) can cause an arbitrary out-of-bounds read, potentially leading to information disclosure or a denial-of-service condition.

hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-48388 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-48388 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-48388, CVE-2026-57256, CVE-2026-91799; vectors: exploit.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-48388.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-48388 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-48388/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-48388 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-48388')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-48388, CVE-2026-57256, CVE-2026-91799; vectors: exploit.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('snort.org','up.exe','netio.sys') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('2.11.0.30') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

article.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-0322 Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Code Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-76519 Cisco Secure Email Gateway Relative Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-105133 Ahsay AhsayCBS Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-105134 Ahsay AhsayCBS Command Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue

article.title: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th)
article.summary: [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]
article.raw_text: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th) [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] Crypto mining malware has been active and spreading across the internet for quite some time now. Moreover, the DShield honeypot picked up a worm that self-propagates through a plethora of means. One of them is stealing SSH keys after it gains access to a system. Furthermore, it also leverages a rootkit to maintain access to infected systems. One would hope that threat actors would have moved on past this worm by now. However, due to its rudimentary design and its effectiveness, they have had no reason to move on. A malicious binary was uploaded and executed on the DShield honeypot, and that is where a copy of the Panchan worm was obtained. It is written with Golang, and it is a peer-to-peer botnet. Moreover, this worm was first identified in 2022. Many vendors recognize this worm now as seen below. VirusTotal Clamscan Therefore, a system with security controls such as egress filtering, ingress filtering, access control lists, continuous monitoring, and passwordless authentication will prevent this worm from taking root. However, many systems are insecure and unpatched. This is why this worm is still propagating across the internet. The strings captured from the binary below show how simple it is to find its command-and-control channel and the functions that it consists of. Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone. Command and Control Channel Panchan Functions These captures clearly show the source files that the Panchan worm consists of. To dig deeper into what this binary can do, a network simulator was used. Moreover, the specific network simulator that was used was FakeNet-NG with Wireshark to intercept the network traffic. These tools were used to identify what URL it was reaching out to once it was installed on a system. FakeNet-NG is a tool developed by the Mandiant FLARE team for dynamic network analysis. This tool simulates legitimate network traffic, allowing an analyst to identify how the malware interacts with the network and if it is communicating with an external server. This specific strain of this worm was using a discord channel as a command-and-control server. This was identified by capturing and dissecting the network traffic that was generated by the worm interacting with the FakeNet-NG network. FAKENET-NG Wireshark Capture Panchan, the peer-to-peer crypto mining worm, is a threat to any organization who has internet facing servers. This worm is mainly a threat to insecure systems, and opening SSH to a public network needs to be done in a secure way. Fail2Ban is a service that scans log files for repeated failed login attempts. This service then blocks that IP address by updating the system’s firewall rule. Fail2Ban is another control that should be put in place with a public facing SSH port. Services like SSH should have multi-factor authentication, and an access control list. The access control list should include specific IP addresses or a jump box. Disabling root login with SSH is another essential security control that needs to be implemented. With SSH, public and private key pairs are another option for authentication. This will then create the capability to disable password authentication for the SSH service preventing brute force attacks. However, these key pairs are often created and forgotten about. This is a security concern, and SSH private keys are something that this worm is designed to steal. Once it has stolen a private key, it attempts to pivot to hosts in the running user’s SSH known_hosts file. A simple mitigation to protect the data within the known_hosts file is to use the HashKnownHosts option within a systems SSH configuration. Furthermore, it is best to mitigate long lived credentials and SSH key stealing by leveraging tools likeHashiCorp Vault to sign SSH certificates with short expirations. This ensures that reusing a key becomes highly impractical or even impossible. The user will authenticate to Vault with their credentials then they send their SSH public key to Vault for signing, and finally Vault then signs the SSH key. Then it returns the SSH certificate to the user. This certificate can be used to log in to any host configured to trust the Vault CA. Leveraging such infrastructure will also allow an organization to disable password authentication entirely for services like SSH. Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone. Typical indicators of compromise for this worm include multiple failed authentication attempts via SSH, unusual resource usage on infected systems, and processes that cannot be killed by any means. This worm also creates hidden directories in the running users home directory or folders like /tmp. Often, these directories have names that are strings that have high amounts of entropy. For this strain of this worm, servers reaching out to services like Discord on a regular basis is another indicator of compromise that an analyst can look for. In conclusion, denying by default and allowing by exception is a vital strategy for systems facing untrusted networks. These same techniques that were discussed above can be used to protect critical public facing infrastructure from threat actors. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. article.title: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-104935)

Ivanti reports that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers. This indicates that exploitation has been occurring as a zero-day vulnerability. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirms exploitation in the wild, and added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day as the vendor's public disclosure. The digital forensics firm Volexity has published a detailed blog post describing the threat actor activity, which was detected in early October 2026. According to the vendor, a portion of the vulnerability was initially discovered through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0 . Exploitation occurred while Ivanti was working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions. Ivanti Connect Secure is a popular enterprise VPN solution and naturally sits on the edge of a corporate env
article.raw_text: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-104935) Overview On October 13, 2026, Ivanti published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104935 , a high-severity authentication bypass by spoofing ( CWE-290 ) affecting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS). The vulnerability has a CVSSv3.0 score of 8.6 and allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. Ivanti reports that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers. This indicates that exploitation has been occurring as a zero-day vulnerability. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirms exploitation in the wild, and added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day as the vendor's public disclosure. The digital forensics firm Volexity has published a detailed blog post describing the threat actor activity, which was detected in early October 2026. Volexity notes that in addition to leveraging CVE-2026-104935 as a zero-day, the threat actor also leveraged an as-yet unpatched privilege escalation vulnerability which Ivanti are planning to patch at a later date. According to the vendor, a portion of the vulnerability was initially discovered through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0 . Exploitation occurred while Ivanti was working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions. Ivanti Connect Secure is a popular enterprise VPN solution and naturally sits on the edge of a corporate environment. The product has a history of being targeted by attackers, with zero-day exploitation of other vulnerabilities occurring back in both 2024 and 2025 . Given the confirmed exploitation, the ability to execute commands without authentication, along with the history of the product, Rapid7 recommends that organizations running affected versions apply the appropriate update on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. Mitigation guidance Vendor-supplied updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-104935. Ivanti lists the following affected and resolved versions: Ivanti Connect Secure affected versions Resolved versions 25.1.1.1 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.1.2 25.1.2.2 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.3.0 , 25.1.3.1 22.8R2.4 and prior in the applicable code line 22.8R2.5 Note that the vendor advisory confirms that versions 22.7.x and below are unaffected. At the time of the advisory, Ivanti states that reliable indicators of compromise are not available, however Volexity have published several here . Rapid7 strongly recommends looking for signs of compromise even after the patch has been applied. Customers who suspect exploitation should follow the vendor's recovery steps . For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the vendor's security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-104935 with a vulnerability check expected to be available in the October 14 content release. Updates October 13, 2026 : Initial publication.

article.title: CVE-2026-21589: Critical unauthenticated arbitrary file access in Atlassian products
article.summary: Overview On October 5, 2026, Atlassian published a security advisory for CVE-2026-21589 , a critical arbitrary file access vulnerability affecting eight products: Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Service Management Data Center, Jira Software Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye. Atlassian assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv4 score of 9.3 . Atlassian's advisory treats all versions before the applicable fixed releases as affected, including unsupported versions. article.raw_text: CVE-2026-21589: Critical unauthenticated arbitrary file access in Atlassian products Overview On October 5, 2026, Atlassian published a security advisory for CVE-2026-21589 , a critical arbitrary file access vulnerability affecting eight products: Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Service Management Data Center, Jira Software Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye. Atlassian assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv4 score of 9.3 . An unauthenticated remote attacker who knows a target file's exact name and path can access it within the application's web root; the vulnerability does not provide directory listing or enumeration. Atlassian's advisory treats all versions before the applicable fixed releases as affected, including unsupported versions. Affected Atlassian Cloud products have already been patched, and no action is required from Cloud customers. Detailed technical analysis and file-read proof-of-concept scripts are public, so Rapid7 recommends patching on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, and reviewing access logs for attempted exploitation. Technical overview NVD lists files or directories accessible to external parties ( CWE-552 ) as the weakness associated with CVE-2026-21589. On October 6, watchTowr Labs published a technical analysis based on comparisons of vulnerable and patched Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket packages. Their analysis identified a path traversal vulnerability in Atlassian's web-resource handling: double-colon ( :: ) sequences can become path separators during request processing, allowing traversal components to reach the resource-loading code, resulting in the contents of arbitrary file being read back to an attacker. Their testing could not traverse outside the Tomcat context, but could read files throughout the application web root. In an Atlassian Crowd deployment that had Jira configured, reading WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties exposed application credentials. With network access to Crowd, they used those credentials to create a user and add it to jira-administrators ; Crowd's IP allowlisting can block this direct route. Mitigation guidance Organizations should upgrade each affected installation to a listed fixed version or the latest available version. Atlassian's October 5 advisory lists the following fixed versions: Product Fixed versions Bitbucket Data Center 9.4.26 , 10.2.8 , 10.5.1 Confluence Data Center 9.2.26 , 10.2.19 Jira Service Management Data Center 5.12.40 , 10.3.26 , 11.3.12 Jira Software Data Center 9.12.40 , 10.3.26 , 11.3.12 Bamboo Data Center 10.2.24 , 12.1.12 Crowd Data Center 6.3.7 , 7.0.3 , 7.1.7 , 7.2.4 Crucible 4.9.15 Fisheye 4.9.15 Organizations unable to patch immediately should remove affected instances from the internet or otherwise restrict them from external network access. Atlassian provides a Web Application Firewall or proxy rule for all affected products, a Tomcat RewriteValve mitigation for Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Bamboo, and Crowd, and a separate urlrewrite.xml rule for Bitbucket. These mitigations are limited and are not replacements for patching. Rapid7 strongly recommends looking for signs of compromise even after the patch has been applied. Atlassian recommends URL-decoding each access-log request line up to twice, then searching for .. immediately adjacent to / , \ , or :: . Alternatively, search raw logs with the vendor-supplied regex: (?is).*(?:/|\\|::|%(?:25)*(?:2f|5c)|(?::|%(?:25)*3a){2})(?:\.|%(?:25)*2e){2}(?:/|\\|::|%(?:25)*(?:2f|5c)|(?::|%(?:25)*3a){2}|;|%(?:25)*3b|$).* Public testing artifacts for Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket include a Python file-read PoC and a Nuclei template . If investigation identifies access to protected configuration files, organizations should rotate exposed credentials and other secrets after containing the affected systems. For the latest mitigation and investigation guidance, please refer to the vendor security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-21589 with unauthenticated vulnerability checks on Jira Software Data Center expected to be available in the October 8 content release. Updates October 7, 2026 : Initial publication.

article.title: More RMM Tools In the Wild, (Tue, Oct 6th)
article.summary: It seems that a trend startedâ€¦ I continue my journey discovering more RMM ("Remote Management & Monitoring") tools abused by threat actors! A few days ago, I wrote a diary[ 1 ] about ScreenConnect used in the wild. Today, I found another one.
article.raw_text: More RMM Tools In the Wild, (Tue, Oct 6th) It seems that a trend startedâ€¦ I continue my journey discovering more RMM ("Remote Management & Monitoring") tools abused by threat actors! A few days ago, I wrote a diary[ 1 ] about ScreenConnect used in the wild. Today, I found another one. It seems that a trend started… I continue my journey discovering more RMM ("Remote Management & Monitoring") tools abused by threat actors! A few days ago, I wrote a diary[ 1 ] about ScreenConnect used in the wild. Today, I found another one. Same scenario, it started with a phishing email that delivers a fake PDF invoice to the victim: When the PDF is opened, it just redirect to a malicious VBS file. Indeed, the PDF contains an “OpenAction” and “URI” keywords, that sounds weird! remnux@remnux:~/files/samples$ pdf-parser.py Transaction\ Receipt\ .pdf -o 3 obj 3 0 Type: /Page Referencing: 1 0 R, 2 0 R, 4 0 R > >> ] /Contents 4 0 R >> The URL will be visited thanks to the OpenAction. This is a common trick to avoid writing URLs in email bodies that can be easily detected. The VBS file is pretty simple and even not obfuscated. It will display another PDF as a decoy: a non-blurred version of the initial attachment. In parallel, a MSI archive will be downloaded and installed: hxxps://up-theta-rose.vercel[.]app/action1.msi The MSI file contains 4 files that are not reported as malicious by VT: $ sha256sum * eaff35d250c9b04f51c971e70082740dbfeee5dd846829d541f588ad43378727 a1_7z_dll_file 996b01e15f85e165899630721a141b178a9c372b6e878012180ec9e9d4e7bd06 a1_sas_dll_file 1b19115d5ebdc216e0ab3adf2c643648cfc70a385f4caf0217c679f9f3b20342 action1_remote_exe 941695d20d82dd5d62f74b0111feb23720637202f6c797df2a02e2cb6cb6e8e3 main_service_exe These files belongs to the RMM tool developed by Action1[ 2 ] and are signed with an "Action1 Corporation" certificate that expired in May 2026. The tool installs itself as a service for persistence ("A1Agent" - "Action1 Agent"), executing C:\Windows\Action1\action1_agent.exe. The registy key "HKLM\Software\Action1\Agent" contains the values: CustomerId, Certificate, PrivateKey, MSI & INSTALLDIR. The CustomerID is: 49b18106-681d-456a-b098-092e2818c09a and is connecting to the Action1 infrastructure via server[.]na-2.action1[.]com. We are facing here the same behaviour: the threat actor abuse the cloud infrastructure of the company developing the RMM tool, probably using a free/test account. [1] https://isc.sans.edu/diary/ScreenConnect+Client+Abused+by+Attackers/33388 [2] https://www.action1.com/remote-access/ Xavier Mertens (@xme) Senior ISC Handler | SANS Principal Instructor | Freelance Consultant Xameco | PGP Key (c) SANS Internet Storm Center. https://isc.sans.edu Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States License.

article.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96951 Microsoft Windows Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-104935 Ivanti Connect Secure Authentication Bypass by Spoofing Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed

CVE-2026-96951 Microsoft Windows Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-104935 Ivanti Connect Secure Authentication Bypass by Spoofing Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as virtual private networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. article.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime
article.summary: Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators (tracked as Storm-2990), and an illicit marketplace (tracked as Storm-3119) selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem. The post The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators (tracked as Storm-2990), and an illicit marketplace (tracked as Storm-3119) selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem. The post The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . In this article Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystem Storm-3119: YAM Store, the power broker Storm-2990: The Iron Man System phishing kit Downstream activity from Storm-2990 phishing kits Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft Defender detections Over the past year, Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing, enabling cybercriminal operations worldwide. Threat actors purchased and used these tools and infrastructure, including phishing kits and access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments and related credentials, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the United States, Australia, and India. In collaboration with law enforcement agencies and other partners worldwide, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) facilitated a disruption of the ecosystem’s primary developers and infrastructure . Microsoft’s research into one phishing kit unraveled a larger ecosystem, including the phishing kit developers, an infrastructure dealer, and the threat actors who buy from both. In this blog, we examine several phishing kits marketed and sold through YAM Store, an underground marketplace tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3119. We share our analysis of the technical aspects of this Chinese-language phishing kit ecosystem, the shared infrastructure, provisioning methods, and downstream activity by threat actors using these tools. Figure 1: Heat map of most impacted countries by combined Storm-3119 and Storm-2990-related activity. Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystem Microsoft, alongside industry partner Resecurity , identified three phishing kits sold through the YAM Store that make up this Chinese-language cybercriminal network: CoGUI (also known as NX or FA), Haozi (also known as Phoenix), and Iron Man System. Microsoft tracks the cluster of activity and the developers behind all three phishing kits as Storm-2990. Since January 2026, the threat actors behind these kits have been responsible for facilitating the sending of over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to over 75 thousand organizations worldwide. Microsoft assesses with high confidence that these phishing kits were developed by Chinese-speaking threat actors, and, despite their distinct branding and separate Telegram-based sales channels, exhibit highly similar capabilities and functionality. The phishing kits provide phishing templates impersonating legitimate brands and organizations (including government, financial, and logistics) worldwide, and enable criminal actors to facilitate high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations. The similarity in their infrastructure and overlap in activity suggest either shared development origins, code reuse, or close collaboration among their developers. These phishing kits have been advertised through YAM Store, first CoGUI and Haozi, followed by Iron Man System starting in June 2026. YAM Store and affiliated phishing kit companies accepted payments through cryptocurrency, including USDT and Ethereum, adding another layer to conceal illicit activity. The scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses. By mapping the relationship between YAM Store and these phishing kits, we provide insight into the commercial infrastructure that supports modern phishing operations. Figure 2. YAM Store (Storm-3119) sells fraudulently acquired infrastructure to CoGUI, Haozi, and Iron Man System, all interconnected phishing kit operators, who then provide these services to other threat actors. Storm-3119: YAM Store, the power broker YAM Store is an initial access broker (IAB) that sells infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google. The marketplace offers a variety of infrastructure based on age, subscription type, and environment types such as education (.edu) or non-profit (.org). Figure 3: YAM Store procurement and downstream activity chain The YAM Store marketplace provides cybercriminals with a platform to purchase fraudulently acquired Microsoft and Google domains associated with legitimate, expired, or previously used organization numbers, allowing actors to use seemingly legitimate infrastructure and obtain workspaces at relatively low cost. Storm-3119 uses automation to identify expired environment or organization names and leverages legitimate customer information associated with them to help circumvent existing detections. Figure 4. YAM Store interface and Telegram contact Anatomy of YAM Store operations: How Storm-3119 acquires, controls, and monetizes infrastructure During this investigation, Microsoft uncovered a five-stage attack pipeline often used in Storm-3119’s operations. YAM Store functions as an access broker, an intermediary that hijacks Microsoft 365 and Azure for Education tenants and resells the stolen accounts, licenses, and storage as a service to downstream operations, including the phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990. The pipeline below describes the supply side of that business: how the actor acquires, controls, and monetizes compromised environments. Stage 1 – Reconnaissance : Storm-3119 conducts automated reconnaissance of target environments. The actor uses Flask, a lightweight Python web framework, to covertly identify and profile cloud-enabled organizations. The tooling is designed to discover Microsoft 365 tenants, assess enrollment opportunities, gather licensing and Azure cloud information, and perform these activities anonymously through Tor infrastructure. Stage 2 – Environment takeover and app-only admin panels : Once a viable environment is identified, the threat actor centralizes associated information in an actor-controlled platform used to administer compromised Microsoft 365 environments. This platform is a separate set of administrative panels (implemented in PHP, Java/Spring, and Cloudflare Workers) that lets the operator maintain, monetize, and expand access using stolen application credentials. Leveraging the compromised environment’s client secret through an application-only authentication flow, the panel performs full directory control: it resets passwords silently (without forcing a change at next sign-in), assigns education licenses, and grants privileged attributes that the actor can later monetize. Because this access is application-level rather than tied to a single user session, the resulting persistence is more durable, more scalable, and harder to detect. Stage 3 – Storage and resource abuse : With the stolen privileged credentials, the threat actor signs in to a compromised Global Administrator account and self-provisions the PnP Management Shell service principal, which represents the actor’s application inside the compromised tenant. Through this service principal, the threat actor grants themselves broad Microsoft Graph permissions, including read and write access to directory data and AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All, along with full control over the SharePoint API. The actor then abuses the compromised tenant’s SharePoint and OneDrive as bulk hosting and converts the hijacked storage into a sellable product. Stage 4 – Phishing and DNS infrastructure support : The threat actor maintains dedicated infrastructure to support and manage phishing operations on behalf of their customers. A custom DNS management platform enables centralized control of phishing domains, SSL certificates, and domain-routing configurations through Cloudflare. Stage 5 – Storefront and monetization : Storm-3119 resells the hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage through an automated storefront, operating as the access broker that supplies these resources to downstream operations. Payment is accepted through Alipay, WeChat Pay, and USDT (TRC20), and the storefront supports a sub-reseller tier. Telegram is used for order notifications and buyer contact rather than as the primary sales channel. In addition to targeting existing tenants, Storm-3119 also separately creates fraudulent organizations and supporting web presence to establish tenants on Microsoft’s platform, likely using AI-generated content and forged documentation to make the fabricated entities appear legitimate. In one case, the actor created an environment, likely using AI, named “Jewish Choice” under the guise of a nonprofit organization and associated it with jewishchoice[.]org , a domain registered only within the past several months that did not appear to represent a legitimate organization. This activity indicates that Storm-3119 likely established the website and associated domain to lend credibility to the fabricated nonprofit identity and facilitate tenant creation. Figure 5: YAM Store created the fake non-profit “Jewish Choice” to sell to criminal actors with a [.]org top-level domain to appear as a legitimate organization in phishing emails. Storm-2990: The Iron Man System phishing kit YAM Store sells its illicitly acquired infrastructure, as well as the prominent phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990, to other threat actors. The platforms are commercially licensed phishing-as-a-service (PaaS) products. They are designed to impersonate organizations across several industry verticals to steal information, including sign-in credentials (usernames, passwords) and financial data (credit card information), used to gain access to network environments. Iron Man System’s customers purchase a subscription that provides access to the kit’s license server, with the domain hard-coded into the kit. This restriction adds a layer of obfuscation by limiting site access to paying customers. The kits allow attackers to steal money by abusing the stolen credit card information. Figure 6. Iron Man System admin sign-in The Iron Man System phishing kit contains over 2,335 templates tailored to over 139 countries including Australia, Japan, India, and the United States, with the United States accounting for the most phishing templates. The phishing lures used by Iron Man System mimic various trusted brands and organizations, such as local government including authorities associated with traffic and parking fees, law enforcement, healthcare, finance, transportation, and retail. These lures are designed to trick targets into providing sensitive information. Most phishing lures used in the United States are transportation or government-related. Figure 7. Phishing lure impersonating traffic authorities in the Philippines Figure 8. Phishing lure impersonating Amazon shipping services Figure 9. Phishing lure impersonating a Japanese financial service provider. It warns the target that a routine security check determined that the target’s account requires re-authentication. The email provides instructions for the target to visit the ‘official’ website and follow instructions to authenticate to the portal Figure 10. Sample lure impersonating Australia Post Figure 11. Sample lure impersonating Medicare The phishing kits are capable of the following advanced evasion techniques to varying degrees: Geofencing , a technique used to restrict access to configured countries only, so only users from specific countries can access the phishing content from their web browser Fake CAPTCHA gates , used to prevent or block automated browsing from threat research tools by making the user click a box or execute an action IP address block list and allow list , used to block or allow IP addresses to prevent threat researcher interaction Anti-detection configuration related tosettings to evade security researcher detection Telegram bot configuration ,including bot tokens and chat IDs for real-time phishing that enables credential exfiltration. It allows the kit operator to receive automatic notifications on their Telegram account when a target takes action on a phishing lure, including entering credentials, credit card data submission, and verification codes. After the target provides the sensitive information (sign-in details, credit card info), the phishing kit collects it using a WebSocket, offering customers real-time victim interaction through Telegram notifications during credential harvesting. This confirms that the kit supports live, interactive phishing where the operator monitors each victim’s progress and manually controls what the victim sees next, a hallmark of sophisticated PaaS platforms. The attacker then harvests the information to use in follow-on fraudulent financial activities. The Iron Man System phishing kit panel is predominately hosted on China-based hosting providers, with a smaller number of panels found on hosting providers in other countries. The fully featured, multi-tenant phishing kit uses the GoFrame application development framework, an open-source Go framework with roots in the Chinese developer ecosystem. Downstream activity from Storm-2990 phishing kits Microsoft observed downstream activity by threat actors using infrastructure affiliated with the Storm-2990 phishing kits. In analyzed cases, the actors used similar common phishing techniques, such as urgency in the message and attaching malicious links that redirect to actor-controlled infrastructure that allows these downstream threat actors to perform the following activities: Credential stealing: The actors use phishing pages that impersonate legitimate services to trick targets into providing credentials or other authentication information, enabling downstream actors to access compromised accounts. Device code phishing: In some cases, the actors abuse the device code authentication flow to trick victims into authenticating to legitimate applications, allowing downstream actors to obtain authentication tokens and access compromised accounts. Financial fraud: The end goal for the downstream actors is to use stolen payment data to make fraudulent purchases of high-end goods or fraudulent transactions on legitimate financial platforms. The threat actors using the phishing kits conduct phishing campaigns at scale whether it is a missing toll payment or a traffic citation. The following screenshots show email or SMS phishing lures used in Storm-2990 phishing kits. Figure 12: Sample of landing pages impersonating mainstream tech, streaming and brokerage services around the world. The templates are tailored to specific countries using trusted local or international brand names and local language. Mitigation and protection guidance This interconnected network of Chinese-language phishing kit operators and developers operates as an enabling ecosystem, providing infrastructure and services that facilitate criminal activity rather than functioning as a standalone malware tool. Microsoft assesses that the ecosystem is not limited to the abuse of Microsoft services and extends to other providers. While Microsoft notes that the identified organizations impacted by attacks stemming from Storm-3119 or Storm-2990 operations include financial, healthcare, and IT companies, the activity conducted by threat actors using these tools are common attacks that could affect any organization. Most of the activity that stems from this phishing kit ecosystem consists of social engineering, phishing operations, and account and storage takeovers. Microsoft recommends the following to mitigate the impact of Storm-3119 and Storm-2990-related threats. In nearly all the cases observed by Microsoft, the phishing lures used by the Storm-2990 operators followed prescriptive scam red flags, including urgency, time-sensitive tasks such as clicking a provided link with official branding. Users should verify with the purported sender of the message or email, even when the task involves signing in to a known, secure account not provided by the link or calling the purported organization or company directly. Educate users about protecting personal and business information in social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lures in spear-phishing emails and watering holes, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activities. Educate users about common phishing techniques. Sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. As of 2021, Microsoft Azure interactions prompt the user to confirm (Cancel or Continue) that they are signing in to the app they expect, which is an option frequently missing from phishing sign-ins. Review our recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity. Configure the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policy to apply to internal recipients. Hardening credentials and cloud identities is also necessary to defend against phishing attacks, which seek to gain valid credentials and access tokens. As an initial step, use passwordless solutions like passkeys and implement multifactor authentication (MFA) throughout your environment: Invoke the principles of least privilege and Zero Trust to significantly slow down threat actors who might have been able to gain initial access and buy time for defenders to respond. Since Storm-3119 operators have been observed obtaining Global Administrator access, implementing these principles can help lock down Global Administrator roles and who has access to specific resources. Use the Microsoft Authenticator app for passkeys and MFA , and complement MFA with Conditional Access policies, where sign-in requests are evaluated using additional identity-driven signals. Conditional Access policies can also be scoped to strengthen privileged accounts with phishing-resistant MFA . Your passkey and MFA policy can be further secured by only allowing MFA and passkey registrations from trusted locations and devices. Enable network protection to prevent applications or users from accessing malicious domains and other malicious content on the internet. Microsoft Defender detections Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. The coverage below applies to the downstream activity detected by Microsoft that was identified using Storm-2990 infrastructure. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage Initial access Storm-2990-affiliated threat actors sign in to compromised accounts. Phishing campaigns use emails with malicious links. Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Atypical travel – Malicious IP address – Unfamiliar sign-in properties Microsoft Defender for Office 365 – A potentially malicious URL click was detected – Email messages containing malicious URL removed after delivery – Email reported by user as malware or phish Microsoft Defender for Cloud – Communication with suspicious domain identified by threat intel Credential access Storm-2990 facilitates high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations. Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Password Spray Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Potential phishing web site – Suspicious activity linked to an emerging threat actor detected – Suspicious connection blocked by network protection Microsoft Defender for Identity – User identity risk elevated based on defender risk assessment – User exhibiting spike in distinct application resource access combinations – User sign-in from shared client infrastructure exhibiting anomalous activity Microsoft Defender XDR – Account compromise through anomalous password spray or credential compromise – Authentication from password-spraying infrastructure – Potential user account compromise identified through attack analysis Microsoft Security Copilot Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports. Customers can also deploy AI agents , including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents , to perform security tasks efficiently: Threat Intelligence Briefing agent Phishing Triage agent Threat Hunting agent Dynamic Threat Detection agent Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Threat Overview Profile: Evolving phishing threats Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about the activity discussed in this blog. article.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-88779 Citrix NetScaler Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . article.raw_text: CVE-2026-97229: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in GitLab Overview On October 12, 2026, GitLab published a critical patch release for CVE-2026-97229 , an integer overflow or wraparound ( CWE-190 ) in the CI/CD regular expression compiler affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). GitLab assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv3.1 score of 10.0 . Under certain conditions, a remote attacker can execute arbitrary code on an affected GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression stored in a malicious CI/CD configuration. While the vendor supplied CVSS score indicates that exploitation is fully unauthenticated, in reproducing the exploit it was noted that an attacker must have a mechanism to plant a malicious CI/CD configuration to a repository prior to triggering the vulnerability. On GitLab instances where new users can self register and create projects, this constraint is removed. The vulnerability affects self-managed GitLab instances across all deployment types. GitLab.com is already running a patched version, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. As of this writing, there is no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-97229. However, Rapid7 Intelligence has independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on an unpatched, official GitLab CE image. Given the vulnerability's maximum CVSS score, network-accessible trigger, and code execution in a GitLab application worker, Rapid7 recommends upgrading affected self-managed instances on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles. Technical overview Rapid7's testing found that an attacker must first be able to commit a malicious CI/CD configuration file .gitlab-ci.yml, and a repository path containing UTF-8 characters to a branch in a public project. For example, an ordinary account can satisfy this prerequisite by creating a public project on a self-managed GitLab instance where that functionality is permitted. The crafted regular expression initially compiles in a compact US-ASCII representation and passes GitLab's regular expression validation. When it is evaluated against a specially formed, valid UTF-8 repository path, Ruby's Onigmo regular expression engine recompiles it for the new encoding after those checks have completed. An integer overflow in the compiler's program-size calculation then causes invalid regular expression instructions to be generated. The resulting loss of control-flow integrity can be used to execute attacker-controlled Onigmo VM operations in the Ruby process and run an operating system command as the GitLab git user. Rapid7 validated the complete chain against the official GitLab 19.4.1 CE Linux amd64 image with address space layout randomization enabled. The same input did not execute against the official patched 19.4.2 CE image. Further root cause and exploit-chain details will be included in a separate Rapid7 technical analysis. Mitigation guidance A vendor-provided patch is available to remediate CVE-2026-97229. Organizations running affected self-managed GitLab CE or EE instances should immediately upgrade to a fixed version, without waiting for a regular patch cycle: Affected GitLab CE/EE versions Fixed version All versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8 19.2.8 All versions from 19.3 before 19.3.5 19.3.5 All versions from 19.4 before 19.4.2 19.4.2 GitLab.com has already been updated, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. Until affected self-managed instances can be upgraded, restricting anonymous access to public projects and preventing untrusted users from creating or writing to public projects can reduce exposure to the exploit path demonstrated by Rapid7. These controls address only the demonstrated delivery path and do not remediate the vulnerable regular expression compiler. For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to GitLab's security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-97229 with an authenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in today’s (October 13) content release. Updates October 13, 2026 : Initial publication.
